The minister admitted it last night, and justified it by saying that Mr. Bennett did the same thing.

That would not be any
answer at all. Anything done ten years ago has no bearing whatever to-day. I do not see how this government can discriminate against the great province of Ontario, which raises almost half the entire taxes of Canada. I do not believe the government can legally discriminate against the greatest taxpayer in this country, as the premier of Ontario says, to the extent that this province will not be able to sell its bonds and carry on its ordinary financing. I assume that applies also to the other provinces, but they can speak for themselves.

Then why complain about
Ontario?

The other provinces can
speak for themselves.
Does the hon. gentleman say the greatest taxpayer or the greatest accumulator?

The province of Ontario does not need any defence on my part, but from time to time it has been attacked from all corners of this house because of the thrift of its business men. It is true that they live in a province where there are natural resources which can be developed. God has given this province water powers and natural resources. I do not see why Ontario should be picked on; after all, it has been a most generous taxpayer, and much of its wealth has gone to compensate the province from which my hon. friend comes.
I am going to try to get this information from the minister in another way. Will he tell the committee how much was collected during the last fiscal year under section 9B (2) ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: What is the anticipated revenue this year? Would it be three times that amount?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The estimate given in my
budget speech was $30,000,000 from the increase, which included the deduction from the interest payable in foreign currency. That is being taken out; and my estimate of the loss due to taking it out was from $8,000,000 to $10,000,000, which would leave an estimate of from $20,000,000 to $22,000,000 for the tax on the interest and dividends payable to nonresidents in Canadian currency.
Amendment agreed to.
Does resolution 10 apply to royalties, rentals and similar payments which may have accrued due before this change became effective?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

Then I should like to point out the discrimination that is brought about in connection with those non-residents who have invested their money in western farm lands. Under the wheat board regulations last year, all the wheat taken off a farm could not be sold, because of the quota restrictions, and in most instances the portion of the crop due to the landlord has not yet been sold; in any event all of it has not been sold. The first proceeds had to go to the tenant in order to provide him with sufficient funds to pay his expenses and carry him over the winter. As a matter of fact, in most instances the landlord was quite pleased to allow him to get his proceeds, because the indications from the wheat board and the government were that all of the crop could be sold by the end of the crop year. If it affects crop proceeds which accrued last fall these non-residents will have to pay the increased tax. Because of their sympathy toward the tenant, or because they simply were not allowed to do so, the tenant having charge of the quota book, these landlords were not able to sell.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: All I can do is take note of the hon. member's observations. I do not know of any way in which the situation can be met.

In this way, may I suggest: it could be applicable at least in connection with agreements of sale of land, or pay-
Income War Tax Act

ments of rent in respect of land which
accrue due only after the change becomes effective.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know how in the world we could investigate that. The operation of this provision is almost automatic. It applies on the money that goes after a certain date. There is no doubt about how much is due the government. But if the deductibility of this amount is to depend upon a question of fact and of law, which will have to be checked, administration will be very difficult. You could not hold it to payments due on western farm land. It would have to apply to the whole range of payments. And I am sure many mistakes would be made. There has to be some definiteness about these things. Very often there will be cases where persons would have escaped the tax had they acted differently.
In this instance I suggest it is the government which might have acted differently.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. member is saying that these people will be penalized for their kind-heartedness. That often happens, unfortunately. There is no intention to be unfair to anybody, but if we do not stick to the simple question whether money is going or not, we will get ourselves into deep water.
I may not have a right perception of the meaning of resolution No. 10. I notice that in the second line it refers to rentals. Would that apply to real property, such as a house?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

I have in mind a case- probably it is too small to mention, but I bring it before the committee because of the principle involved. I knew a family, the parents of which are now dead. They lived in a small Ontario town north of Toronto. They had one daughter. The daughter married an American-well, I do not know whether he was an American, but at any rate he lived in the United States. She and her husband now live in that country, and have been there for years. When the parents passed away they left her their small house. From it there is an income of $8 a month, or $96 a year. I am told the taxes are approximately $32 a year, leaving a balance of some $64 from the total rental. Do I understand that before that $64 could be sent to the United States, fiften per cent would be deducted from the rent?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The 15 per cent would be taken from the total rental.

Off the whole of the $96?
[Mr. Bence 1

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

That makes it far worse than I had thought. I think I shall stick to my figures, because they do not seem so bad. Taking 15 per cent off the net of $64 would bring the net down to $54.40. When the money is sent across the border the person who looks after the estate will have to pay 10 per cent exchange, which will bring the total down to $48.96. Now, the owner has to call in a plumber once in a while, and she will have to make other repairs. There will be nothing left for her. I am not speaking for the big corporations,- because they can afford to pay. I am speaking, rather, of a small house owner who will have little left if the 15 per cent is taken off the total amount, which in this instance is $96. Fifteen per cent of that amount would be roughly $14, and that sum added to payments for taxes and repairs would leave very little. It seems to me that this provision is unfair to the small house owner.

I should like to discuss further a point I mentioned yesterday. On the Pacific coast there are many instances in which, after the tax is levied on the gross rental, there is no net rental left; in other words all the rent is eaten up, and the owners have to provide a portion of the tax from capital account. That is unfair, and I repeat that the minister ought to consider incorporating in the resolution an exemption providing that when there is no net rental left, in the imposition of the tax, no further tax should be imposed. In other words, do not go beyond the net rental. Allow the owner to deduct his taxes, repairs, insurance, and charges of the kind.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This is a matter of administration. If we have to have an accounting of these cases to get returns from persons resident in the United States and Great Britain, we have very little control over them, and cannot send in our auditors, or anything of that sort. The only way to control such a situation is to take a proportion of the gross. I do not think it should be computed on the net basis. In my opinion it should remain on the gross basis. If the hon. member were suggesting a rate of five per cent, or stating that it should not go up to 15 per cent, his contention would be administrable and practical. But I do not think it is desirable to move from the gross to the net basis in regard to this class of payment of non-resident. As I said last night, the United States does not do it, and I believe for the same reason we are not doing it.

I am not suggesting the minister should leave the gross basis. If he

Income War Tax Act
wishes, let him continue on that basis; but do not take more than the net rent a man receives. The department collects this tax on rentals anyway, from the agents in Canada.
I understand that is the way the money is collected. The agent has to pay it to the government, so that there could be no further administrative difficulty in getting a statement from the agent as to the expenses. Let the agent claim for certain expenses-for municipal taxes, insurance and repairs which have to be paid out in connection with a property. There is no reason why that information could not be obtained.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We would have to go into the amounts paid by his principal as well as the amounts paid by himself. That is, we cannot take merely the amount that he happens to pay out personally, and assert a sort of jurisdiction over the agent. We have to deal with the person in interest, the owner of the property. And if we are going to move to this other basis we have to see what he receives from the house and pays out in respect of it. That would include many things, possibly, that the agent does not pay.

You find that out now from the agent. You find out what rental is paid, and you make the agent responsible for paying five per cent of the gross rental. If the regulation goes through it will mean that the government will collect IS per cent from the agent on the gross rental.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
Why can the department not find out from the agent the expenses in connection with the property, and then make such provision that the owner will not have to pay the tax out of his capital?

There is jurisdiction here over the property. This is an income tax to be collected from the owner, whether it be a corporation or an individual, and the minister has jurisdiction because the properties would be within the territorial jurisdiction of the country. He could place restrictions against the agents and they would have to conform with the regulations before they could pay anything to the owner. I do not see that there is anything wrong with that from the administrative standpoint. However, I think it is objectionable to take 15 per cent of the gross rental or gross income. I should like to know anyone who is getting 15 per cent on his real estate to-day. I have some, and I would be delighted to have half of that left after paying the carrying charges, the taxes, and for all the other things that tenants want. If I could get four per cent 14873-184
net after allowing proper depreciation, I would be happy. We used to try to get six per cent, but you cannot get that to-day. You cannot raise rents, and the cost of everything you put into a property has gone up, including taxes. The minister is taking 15 per cent of the gross rentals on real estate, which is just robbery.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is talking about the percentage on the value of the property, whereas this is concerned with a percentage of the rental.
If you take 15 per cent of the rental you take all th6 cream and leave the owner just the skim-milk.

This will work a hardship in many cases. I know of a house in Toronto which is being rented for $60 a month. In one year, after mortgage interest and other carrying charges had been paid, there was a net return of $14. The total rental at $60 a month would be $720, and 15 per cent of that would be $108. I do not think we have jurisdiction to tax something which is not income. Property is under the jurisdiction of the provinces, and in order to pay this tax it might be necessary to dispose of the property.

It is not very often that I rise in my place to say something in support of property holders, but I must say I am surprised at the attitude taken by the Minister of Finance in view of his concern on other occasions for certain vested interests. It is obvious that this is not a tax on income, it is a tax on revenue. If we cannot tax these people on their ordinary income, surely we cannot tax them on the revenue received. It seems to me that that is quite unfair. The function of a tax is to tax the income of the people, to take that which they are not using for living expenses or to maintain a reasonable standard of living. A non-resident of Canada gets a certain rent and it is quite possible that that rent is eaten up in the upkeep of the property, yet you are charging a tax on the rent received. I do not think it is fair.

Subsection 4 of section 27 of the Income War Tax Act provides for payment by the agent of the non-resident. Would it not be possible to provide for a return by the agent showing the proper expenses in connection with the maintenance of the property?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
In many cases the non-resident owner of the property will himself pay the mortgage interest and insurance. The

Income War Tax Act

agent would have no power to compel his principal to give him that information, and we would have no power to penalize the agent for giving wrong information because it would be information which he would receive from someone else and of which he would have no personal knowledge. It is fairly easy to administer an income tax upon persons within the jurisdiction, and we do it; but it is quite difficult to administer such a tax against persons outside the jurisdiction and that is why we are imposing this one on the gross payments.

Why not leave the rate at five per cent in this case? Would that affect the revenue to any great extent?
Mr. 1LSLEY: If an exception is to be made here and the rate is brought down to five per [DOT] cent, the same thing will have to be done with certain other clauses in this section. Just as sure as I am standing here, if I proposed an extension of the five per cent rate to other forms I would be attacked just as strongly as I am being urged to take this action now. I do not think that I had better consider that. Undoubtedly there will be cases of hardship, but there is one escape, by incorporation in the country.
Mr. JACKMAN; Provided it is a big enterprise.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I suppose it would be pretty hard to get around it in some of the smaller cases, but small companies can be formed. If we made a breach in our 15 per cent rate, the same rate would have to be applied to other remittances made under this section. It would have to be applied all along the line, whereupon I would be attacked most strongly by those persons who are so anxious about the national defence tax and so on. I think the only thing I can do is to leave it alone.
Could provision not be made for an owner to apply for a rebate? In other words, he could pay the tax on the gross rental and then apply for rebate.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not think we could stop here. Has the receiver of rents a better right to file a return and set up deductions, expenses and so on, than the receiver of interest, the receiver of royalties, or the receiver of any other form of payment? That would put us into the business of controlling, checking and auditing the affairs of non-residents.

The position is different, because the man who receives interest or royalty payments does not have to pay out

any money; it is a net amount that he receives.
Progress reported.
